timeline.description: Sixteen-year-old Nissim Zacouto turns a batch of his father's oriental rugs into an established wholesale carpet business at Jäger Strasse 61.
timeline.longDescription: In the early 20th century, business relations between the Ottoman Empire and the German Reich blossomed in the wake of the newly constructed railroad to Baghdad, and oriental products were very fashionable. Sixteen-year-old Nissim Zacouto quickly and profitably sold a batch of oriental rugs sent to Berlin by his father Isaac, a carpet and antique dealer in Constantinople. A year later he settled permanently in Berlin and entered a carpet business under his name in the commercial register. The business moved from Heiliggeist Strasse to an exclusive property at Jäger Strasse 61 and concentrated entirely on wholesale, supplying leading department stores and renowned specialist outlets. Zacouto became vice president and interim president of the Turkish-German chamber of commerce. A 1926 smuggling investigation proved unfounded – the chamber of commerce called his firm 'one of the few decent Turkish firms'. In the early 1930s he weathered a huge drop in the oriental rug trade caused by the world economic crisis.

timeline.description: Protected as a Turkish national but strangled by foreign exchange controls and a branch insider's slander, Zacouto shifts his business abroad.
timeline.longDescription: As one of about 600 Turkish nationals in Berlin, Zacouto was technically protected from direct attacks on his person and business. But his reliance on foreign exchange to import merchandise placed him in a vulnerable position: after 1931 the Reich mark was subject to a complicated system of clearing and allotment rigorously applied by the Reich bank and the exchange control agencies. Joachim Quantmeyer, district head of the 'Reich specialist group for carpets, furnishing textiles and curtains', made a statement colored by anti-Semitic prejudice – slander by a branch insider that increasingly limited Zacouto's scope for doing business. Seeking an alternative, he gradually transferred his business abroad, settling on France from 1935-36. Prevented from conducting foreign trade in Berlin, he began retailing pre-war stock, advertising in the German Carpet Trade Gazette until 1938 – some customers were now Jewish emigrants hoping to transfer expensive bucharas or shirvans abroad as simple rugs.

timeline.description: Zacouto emigrates to France, survives in hiding in the Pyrenees, and rebuilds his carpet business in postwar Paris.
timeline.longDescription: In 1939, Nissim Zacouto emigrated with his family, leaving his Berlin business behind as security. He acquired status as a Protégé Spécial Français, which enabled him to transfer a considerable part of his assets abroad. After the outbreak of war he was deemed a national of an enemy country, and the 'Reich commissioner for the treatment of enemy assets' appointed Hermann Hänecke administrator of his business in March 1940; after France's occupation, the receiver had the business deleted from the Berlin commercial register in March 1941. Zacouto fled Paris for Nice in 1940 and, to avoid the Gestapo, went into hiding with his family on the farm of a school friend of his wife in the Pyrenees.

timeline.description: Zacouto rebuilds his carpet business in postwar Paris; restitution was never concluded. Galeries Lafayette stands on the site today.
timeline.longDescription:
On France's liberation, the Zacoutos returned to Paris, where Nissim ran a carpet business to an advanced age. In the 1950s he considered reviving his business in Berlin, but when several costly and time-consuming compensation appeals failed, he stayed in Paris where he again built up a successful carpet trading business. The restitution of the Berlin business assets has never been concluded. Nissim Zacouto died in 1987; his wife Norma in 1997. In 2010/11 a biography of Nissim Zacouto was published in English, German and Turkish.

The site today

Today the department store Galeries Lafayette stands on the site of Jäger Strasse 61 and the adjacent land in Berlin-Mitte, where Zacouto's exclusive wholesale carpet showroom once operated.
